overview: Sigma 4.11's FriendAlert is a purely passive tab-list watcher: it registers for EventPacket, filters incoming packets to S38PacketPlayerListItem, and when the server broadcasts an ADD_PLAYER action it walks the AddPlayerData list, matches each name against FriendManager.isFriend, and posts a 2.5-second notification when a friend appears. The module constructs no packets, mutates no packet fields, and never responds to the server - its entire effect is a client-side toast. Because the data it reads is server-initiated broadcast traffic that every client receives anyway, there is no server-observable behavior to distinguish a FriendAlert user from a vanilla client, which makes it the archetype of an undetectable read-only module.

sections.p: The trigger is S38PacketPlayerListItem with Action.ADD_PLAYER, the packet the server sends to every player in the tab list when someone joins (and the same packet family used for game-mode and latency updates). FriendAlert ignores every other action and every other packet type, so it fires exactly once per join broadcast. The per-entry match is FriendManager.isFriend(name), which compares case-insensitively after stripping control codes and always returns true for the local player's own profile name - the self-entry in the tab list is the only guaranteed match. The notification text is the friend's name in aqua (§b) with a 2500ms lifetime and Type.INFO, and the unused connect/currentY/targetY/Timer fields are leftovers from an earlier draft that never shipped.

The module's server-visible footprint is zero: it sits on the incoming side of the packet bus (ep.isIncoming()), reads only fields the vanilla client would read to render the tab list, and produces nothing on the outgoing side. No anticheat check in the corpus attaches any behavior to S38PacketPlayerListItem - the packet is presentational state synchronization, not a client-behavior probe. The only way the module could be observed is if a modified variant acted on the harvested names (chat messages, tab-complete probes, friend-targeted attacks), and that would be a different module. FriendAlert itself is a textbook demonstration that information-only modules are undetectable by design, which is why its countering section documents the server-side lifecycle of the S38 data instead of a detection that does not exist.

files.label: FriendAlert.java (module)
files.explanation: The handler is a single instanceof filter: ep.isIncoming() && ep.getPacket() instanceof S38PacketPlayerListItem, then a second filter on func_179768_b() == Action.ADD_PLAYER. The per-entry loop iterates packet.func_179767_a() (the AddPlayerData list), extracts data.field_179964_d.getName(), and posts the notification through Notifications.getManager().post when FriendManager.isFriend returns true. Everything the module touches is read-only: the packet, the friend list, and the notification manager. The vestigial fields (connect, name, currentY, targetY, timer) are declared but never used, and there is no onEnable/onDisable, so the module's runtime cost is one packet-type check per incoming packet.

files.label: FriendManager.java (friend list source)
files.explanation: FriendManager is the lookup table behind the alert. It keeps a static ArrayList<Friend> persisted to a 'Friends' config file as name:alias lines (load() splits on ':' and save() rewrites the file), and isFriend(name) is the matcher FriendAlert calls: it iterates the list comparing friend.name against StringUtils.stripControlCodes(name) with equalsIgnoreCase, and hard-codes the local player's own game profile name as always-friend. That last rule is why the tab-list self-entry can produce an alert even with an empty friend list. Because the comparison strips color codes and ignores case, the module matches names regardless of how the server formats them in the S38 payload.

countering.label: PacketEntityReplication (the AC's only S38 consumption)
countering.explanation: Grim's PacketEntityReplication is the representative example of what a modern anticheat actually does with S38PacketPlayerListItem: it parses ADD_PLAYER entries (WrapperPlayServerPlayerInfo / PlayerInfoUpdate) to register UUIDs and positions into its compensatedEntities bookkeeping, and REMOVE_PLAYER to unregister them - the same data FriendAlert reads, consumed for entity-replication state rather than for client-behavior detection. The handler treats the packet as authoritative server state about other entities, never as evidence about the receiving client. That is the entire point of the comparison: FriendAlert performs an identical parse on the client side and then does nothing observable with it. There is no counter to measure, because the AC's ledger is keyed to the packet's content, not to who read it or when - a read leaves no trace in any server-side data structure.

countering.label: SpectateManager (S38 filtering predicate)
countering.explanation: SpectateManager holds the predicate that decides which tab-list entries get hidden from which viewers: shouldHidePlayer(receiver, uuid) returns true when the entry is a spectator (or on the hidden list), the receiver is not themselves a spectator, and the world filter passes. This is presentation logic over the same S38 stream FriendAlert watches - the AC decides what the client should see, but it cannot and does not infer anything about what the client does with what it sees. The function's inputs are receiver identity, entry UUID and world configuration; a client that renders the entry and pops a notification is indistinguishable from a client that renders nothing. The check documents the boundary of the packet's trust model: servers filter S38 content on the way out because it is display data, and display data carries no return channel for detection.

countering.label: PacketHidePlayerInfo (S38 rewriting)
countering.explanation: PacketHidePlayerInfo is the outbound half of the same machinery: on PLAYER_INFO (S38) sends it rewrites ADD_PLAYER and UPDATE_GAME_MODE entries for spectated targets - faking spectator game modes back to survival, re-encoding the packet, or cancelling it outright when every entry was hidden. The key fact for FriendAlert is that the AC itself modifies and cancels S38 packets before delivery, which means the packet is treated as untrusted presentation state whose only server-side counterpart is the broadcast itself. A client-side reader of that stream generates no traffic the server could correlate: the ADD_PLAYER broadcast is already happening, the read is passive, and the notification never leaves the process. The one theoretical counter - detecting clients that acknowledge or re-request tab-list data - would require the client to send something, and FriendAlert never does.
